title: Weimar Germany, 1919–1933: a Survey
description: Versailles, Weimar’s early crises, Stresemann’s recovery and the Depression that destroyed German democracy.
content_html:
Germany After the First World War

When Germany signed the armistice in November 1918, the Kaiser abdicated and a new democratic republic was proclaimed. The new government inherited enormous problems: a nation exhausted by four years of war, millions of dead and wounded, and a people who had been told the war was going well right up until the defeat. Many Germans felt humiliated and confused by the sudden collapse.

The Weimar Republic took its name from the city where its constitution was written in 1919. Germany’s new constitution created one of the most democratic systems in the world at that time, with universal suffrage — votes for all adults — and proportional representation in the Reichstag. It also included Article 48, which allowed the president to govern by emergency decree without consulting parliament, a clause that would later be fatally misused.

Key Fact

The Treaty of Versailles (1919) forced Germany to accept war guilt (Article 231), pay reparations set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921 (about £6.6 billion at the time), lose 13% of its territory and 10% of its population, and reduce its army to 100,000 men.

The Treaty of Versailles and Its Impact

Signed in June 1919, the Treaty of Versailles caused immediate outrage in Germany. The ‘war guilt’ clause (Article 231) forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for the war. Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France, the Polish Corridor was created dividing East Prussia from the rest of Germany, and the Rhineland was demilitarised and occupied by Allied troops. German colonies were handed to the victorious powers as League of Nations mandates. Many Germans called the settlement a ‘Diktat’ — a dictated peace — imposed without any German input in negotiations.

Politicians who signed the armistice and accepted Versailles were labelled ‘November criminals’ by nationalist critics. This stab-in-the-back myth — the idea that Germany had been betrayed from within, not defeated in battle — became a powerful propaganda weapon against the Weimar Republic throughout its existence.

Early Crises: Left and Right Challenges

The Weimar Republic faced violent challenges from both left and right almost immediately. In January 1919, the Spartacist Rising attempted to establish a Soviet-style republic in Berlin. The government used the Freikorps — irregular right-wing soldiers — to crush the revolt; its leaders, Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, were murdered. This decision embedded deep hostility between the Social Democrats and the German communist left.

In March 1920, the Kapp Putsch brought a challenge from the right. Wolfgang Kapp led Freikorps troops to seize Berlin, declaring the Weimar government overthrown. The army refused to act against the rebels. The putsch failed only because Berlin workers called a general strike, paralysing the capital. The republic had been saved by the workers, not the military — revealing how fragile its institutional loyalties were.

In November 1923, at the height of the economic crisis, Adolf Hitler led the Nazi Party in an attempted coup in Munich. He believed the moment of maximum chaos was the right time to seize power. The putsch collapsed when police opened fire on the marchers; sixteen Nazis and four police officers were killed. Hitler was arrested and sentenced to five years in prison, though he served only nine months. During his imprisonment he wrote Mein Kampf. The failure of the putsch convinced Hitler that power had to be won through elections, not armed uprising.

Hyperinflation 1923

Germany’s economy was already under severe strain from reparations payments when, in January 1923, France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr industrial region, claiming Germany had defaulted on timber deliveries. The Weimar government ordered passive resistance — workers refused to cooperate with the occupiers but needed to be paid. The government printed money to fund the campaign, triggering catastrophic hyperinflation.

By November 1923 a loaf of bread cost billions of marks. Savings accumulated over decades were wiped out almost overnight. Those on fixed incomes — pensioners, civil servants — were ruined. People carried money in wheelbarrows to buy basic goods. The psychological impact of hyperinflation on the German middle class was lasting: it generated a deep distrust of the democratic republic and its ability to manage the economy.

Key Fact

Stresemann’s recovery in 1923–24 rested on three pillars: ending passive resistance in the Ruhr, replacing the worthless mark with a new currency (the Rentenmark), and negotiating the Dawes Plan (1924) to reschedule reparations with US loans.

Stresemann and the Golden Twenties

Gustav Stresemann served as chancellor briefly in 1923 and then as foreign minister until his death in October 1929. He ended passive resistance in the Ruhr, stabilised the currency, and set Germany on a path of recovery. The Dawes Plan of 1924 brought American loans and restructured reparations, allowing industry to recover. US investment poured into Germany throughout the mid-1920s, funding factories, housing and infrastructure.

Internationally, Stresemann pursued a policy of diplomatic engagement. The Locarno Pact of 1925 normalised Germany’s western borders and improved relations with France and Britain. In 1926 Germany joined the League of Nations as a permanent member of the Council — a major rehabilitation of German international standing. The Young Plan of 1929 further reduced reparations. Germany appeared, by the late 1920s, to be a stable democracy integrating into the international community.

The mid-1920s saw a cultural flourishing in Weimar Germany. Berlin became a centre of modern art, cabaret, cinema and experimental theatre. The Bauhaus design school pioneered modernist architecture and craft. Yet this cultural openness was resented by conservative and nationalist Germans who saw it as immoral and un-German. Weimar stability was also more fragile than it appeared: the economy depended on short-term American loans, the political parties rarely cooperated effectively, and extremist parties — both Nazi and Communist — continued to win seats in the Reichstag.

The Depression and the Collapse of Weimar

Stresemann’s death in October 1929 came at the worst possible moment. Weeks later, the Wall Street Crash triggered a global economic depression. American banks recalled their loans to Germany, businesses collapsed and unemployment soared: by early 1932 approximately six million Germans were out of work. The economic catastrophe destroyed the fragile consensus that had sustained Weimar democracy during the recovery years.

Weimar’s proportional representation system produced fragmented parliaments where coalition governments struggled to agree. Between 1930 and 1932 chancellors governed increasingly by emergency decree under Article 48, bypassing the Reichstag. Support for the Nazi Party surged: in the 1928 election the Nazis won under 3% of the vote; by July 1932 they were the largest party with 37.4%. In January 1933, President Hindenburg appointed Hitler as chancellor, believing conservative advisers could control him. That miscalculation ended the Weimar Republic.
exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark period essay, you need a substantiated overall judgement — not just a list of factors. A strong answer on Weimar Germany will weigh why the republic fell when it did: how far the Depression was more decisive than the republic’s structural weaknesses, or how far Versailles created conditions that made failure likely from the start. Use specific dates and evidence (e.g. the Dawes Plan 1924, July 1932 election result, Article 48 emergency decrees) to anchor each point. Finish with a clearly argued judgement. For 6-mark cause or consequence questions, explain the mechanism of the cause — don’t just describe the event.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Weimar Republic was born in crisis: the Treaty of Versailles (1919) imposed war guilt, reparations and territorial losses that fuelled nationalist resentment and undermined faith in democracy from the start.
  • The republic survived early crises — Spartacist Rising (1919), Kapp Putsch (1920), hyperinflation (1923), Munich Putsch (1923) — before a period of relative stability under Stresemann, 1924–1929, built partly on fragile US loans.
  • The Wall Street Crash (1929) and the Great Depression destroyed Weimar’s economic recovery, produced mass unemployment, and drove voters to extremes. Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933, ending the republic.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Treaty of Versailles (1919) and its impact on Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• The War Guilt Clause (Article 231) forced Germany to accept sole responsibility for the First World War. This caused widespread anger among Germans, who felt the clause was unjust and used it to label the Weimar politicians who signed the treaty as ‘November criminals’. [2 marks]
• Germany was required to pay reparations, eventually set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921 (about £6.6 billion at the time). This placed a severe burden on the German economy and contributed to the financial crises of the early 1920s. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for a simple identification with no development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the crisis year 1923 in Weimar Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Simple identification of two features with basic description.
Secure: Each feature is described with relevant context, e.g.:
• The French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in January 1923, following Germany’s failure to deliver reparations goods, led the government to call for passive resistance, which was funded by printing money and triggered hyperinflation. [2 marks]
• Hitler’s Munich Putsch in November 1923 was an attempt to seize power during the economic crisis. It failed when police opened fire; sixteen Nazis were killed and Hitler was arrested and imprisoned. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the rise of the Nazi Party between 1929 and 1932.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: A simple statement of a cause with little explanation.
Developing: Cause identified with some explanation of the mechanism.
Secure: Clear explanation of how the cause led to Nazi growth, with specific evidence.
Mastering: Analytical explanation that considers the mechanism in depth, using precise data (e.g. unemployment figures, election percentages).
Example content: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 caused American banks to recall loans to Germany, leading to rapid industrial collapse and mass unemployment. By early 1932 approximately six million Germans were out of work. This created desperation and resentment that the Nazis exploited, offering scapegoats (Jews, communists, the Weimar government) and promises of strong leadership. Nazi support rose from under 3% in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the hyperinflation crisis of 1923 for the Weimar Republic.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification of a consequence.
Developing: Consequence described with some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the long-term significance of the consequence beyond 1923.
Example content: Hyperinflation wiped out the savings of the German middle class — pensioners and civil servants on fixed incomes lost everything overnight. This created lasting hostility towards the Weimar Republic, as many blamed democratic politicians for the crisis. Even after Stresemann stabilised the currency, the memory of 1923 left many middle-class Germans distrustful of democracy and susceptible to extremist parties that promised stability and strong government.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Stresemann’s policies for the Weimar Republic in the years 1923–1929.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of what Stresemann did.
Developing: Some assessment of importance with limited analysis.
Secure: Explains significance at the time AND over time, using evidence.
Mastering: Weighs immediate recovery against the underlying fragility; argues how far Stresemann’s achievements masked structural weaknesses.
Content to use: Stresemann ended passive resistance, introduced the Rentenmark, negotiated the Dawes Plan (1924) and Locarno Pact (1925), and secured League of Nations membership (1926). At the time these restored economic confidence and international respectability. Over time, however, the recovery rested on short-term US loans, meaning Germany’s prosperity was fragile and dependent on continued American investment — exposed when the Depression struck in 1929.

practice_questions.text:
'The Weimar Republic was doomed to fail from the start because of the Treaty of Versailles.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
In your answer, consider both reasons to agree and reasons to disagree, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Limited points, mostly descriptive, no overall judgement.
Developing: Some argument for and against, limited use of evidence, weak conclusion.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence for both sides, clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Sophisticated argument that weighs the relative importance of Versailles against other factors (structural flaws of the constitution, Depression, political miscalculations), reaches a substantiated conclusion.

Arguments to agree: War guilt caused immediate resentment; reparations destabilised the economy; the ‘November criminals’ myth delegitimised the republic; territorial losses fuelled nationalism.
Arguments to disagree: The republic survived Versailles and the crises of 1919–1923; Stresemann’s era (1924–1929) showed democracy could work; it was the contingent factor of the Depression combined with poor political decisions in 1930–1933 that actually destroyed the republic.

flashcard_questions.a: Germany’s democratic government, 1919–1933, named after the city where its constitution was drafted.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles require?
flashcard_questions.a: Germany to accept sole war guilt for the First World War.

flashcard_questions.q: What were reparations set at in 1921?
flashcard_questions.a: 132 billion gold marks in 1921 (about £6.6 billion at the time).

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Spartacist Rising and who led it?
flashcard_questions.a: January 1919; led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the Kapp Putsch of 1920 fail?
flashcard_questions.a: Berlin workers called a general strike, paralysing the capital.
The government printed money to pay workers during the French occupation of the Ruhr.
A new stable currency introduced in late 1923 to replace the worthless mark.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Dawes Plan (1924) achieve?
flashcard_questions.a: It brought US loans to Germany and restructured reparations payments.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Locarno Pact (1925) establish?
flashcard_questions.a: Germany accepted its western borders with France and Belgium, improving international relations.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Germany join the League of Nations?

flashcard_questions.a: The false claim that Germany was betrayed by politicians and civilians in 1918, not defeated in battle.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Nazi vote share in the July 1932 Reichstag election?
flashcard_questions.a: 37.4%, making the Nazis the largest party in the Reichstag.

glossary_terms.definition: Germany’s democratic government 1919–1933, established after the Kaiser’s abdication, named after the city where its constitution was drafted.
The 1919 peace settlement that ended the First World War, imposing war guilt, reparations, territorial losses and military restrictions on Germany.
A communist uprising in Berlin in January 1919, led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, crushed by the Freikorps.
The catastrophic collapse of the German mark’s value in 1923, when prices rose so fast that money became nearly worthless.
A 1924 agreement that restructured German reparations payments and provided American loans, enabling economic recovery.
A 1925 set of treaties normalising Germany’s western borders and improving its relations with France, Britain and Belgium.
The false nationalist claim that Germany had not been defeated militarily in 1918 but had been betrayed by politicians on the home front.
A clause of the Weimar Constitution allowing the president to rule by emergency decree, bypassing the Reichstag, which was misused after 1930.
